# The In-Package Assistant {#ai-in-package}

The [external-agent path](#ai-driver) has the package acting as an engine and you as the planner. This chapter covers the other arrangement: the package also writes the plan, by asking a language model what to do.

That convenience is real, and so is its price. `sclet` needs `aisdk`, a configured provider, and a network call for every plan. The chunks here are therefore gated on `SCLET_BOOKDOWN_EVAL_AI` rather than on the package alone: on a machine with a provider configured they execute and the outputs below are real, and on a machine without one — a CI runner, most of them — they are skipped. Rendered prose that depends on a model's mood is not a regression test, and a build that quietly spends credits is not a build.

## Requirements

```{r ai-in-package-setup, include=FALSE}
# NOTE: `eval_ai` (defined in index.Rmd) is TRUE only when
# SCLET_BOOKDOWN_EVAL_AI is set AND aisdk is installed. Everything below runs
# for real when it is, and skips without failing when it is not.
#
# Not every chunk here needs a model. Building `demo` and running the
# integration that the audit compares against are ordinary computation, so they
# are gated on `eval_chunks` and execute on every render; only the five chunks
# that actually call a provider are gated on `eval_ai`. Keeping the split
# explicit means `render-record.md` shows which of this chapter's work was
# verified without a network, and which needed SCLET_BOOKDOWN_EVAL_AI.
```

```{r ai-in-package-config, eval=eval_ai}
library(sclet)

# A default model, configured once through aisdk:
aisdk::get_model()

# Everything else works without any further setup. `NULL` here means the
# default, which is to inject the shipped skills; `getOption()` is used rather
# than `options()` because the latter evaluates an unset name and errors.
getOption("sclet.ai.use_skills")
```

`options(sclet.ai.use_skills)` controls whether the shipped skills are injected into the planning prompt. It is on by default, and the [AI foundations](#ai-foundations) chapter explains why the skills — not the inline prompt — carry knowledge-type rules such as stage ordering.

## An object to ask about

The examples below need an object with clusters to find markers in, and — for the audit section — an integration that exposes a corrected expression layer. Building both here keeps the chapter self-contained:

```{r ai-in-package-object, eval=eval_chunks}
set.seed(42)
demo <- scuttle::mockSCE(ncells = 200, ngenes = 60)
demo <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = SummarizedExperiment::assay(demo, "counts")),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(demo))
)
demo$batch <- rep(c("donor_1", "donor_2"), each = 100)

demo <- NormalizeData(demo)
demo <- FindVariableFeatures(demo)
demo <- ScaleData(demo)
demo <- RunPCA(demo, ncomponents = 10)
demo <- FindNeighbors(demo, dims = 1:10)
demo <- FindClusters(demo, resolution = 1.0)
demo$ident <- as.character(SingleCellExperiment::colLabels(demo))

length(unique(demo$ident))
```

## `AIPlanAnalysis`: ask for a plan

```{r ai-in-package-plan, eval=eval_ai, warning=FALSE}
plan <- AIPlanAnalysis(demo, goal = "find markers that distinguish the clusters")

plan$actions
```

You will see a warning on the way, and it is the privacy layer doing its job rather than a problem:

> `sclet AI outbound payload requires user consent before use. Fields requiring consent were redacted: active_states.clustering, features.hvg.selected`

Those two fields are the clustering and the selected variable features. Both are *results* of the analysis, not inputs to it, so they are held back unless you say otherwise — the point of the ledger is that a model can plan the next step without being handed the answer. The plan above is still correct because it does not need them: "find markers that distinguish the clusters" is a goal, and the cluster labels are read locally at execution time. If a later round does need the feature set, pass `privacy_consent = TRUE` to the call that makes it, and know that you have chosen to share it.

The result is an ordinary plan — the same structure you wrote by hand in the previous chapter — so it is validated, previewed and executed by exactly the same functions. `AIPlanAnalysis()` also spends one repair round against validation errors and goal coverage before returning, so what you get back has already been checked once. `plan$metadata$goal_coverage$missing` names goal items with no step behind them; a hand-written plan gets no such help, so check it yourself.

### The registry has to match the goal

`AIPlanAnalysis()` plans against every action group by default. `RunAIAnalysis()` differs: it defaults to a *beginner* registry — read, preprocess, dimred, graph, cluster — which is the right set for "run a pipeline from raw counts" and the wrong one for "find markers", because `run_de_test` lives in the `annotation` group.

What that costs you is worth watching once, because the failure is instructive rather than silent. With the beginner registry the planner is shown only its eleven actions, so for a marker goal it proposes a step it was never offered, and validation refuses the plan:

> `action is not registered: run_de_test; it exists, but in the 'annotation' registry group, which this registry did not request -- add 'annotation' to include`

Two things are true at once here. The registry you pass **is** part of the question — pass the groups your goal needs. And the engine's refusal tells you exactly how to fix it, because a bare "not registered" would have sent you looking for a typo.

## `RunAIAnalysis`: plan, preview, ask, execute in one call

```{r ai-in-package-run, eval=eval_ai, warning=FALSE}
result <- RunAIAnalysis(demo, goal = "find markers that distinguish the clusters",
    include = c("read", "preprocess", "dimred", "graph", "cluster", "annotation"),
    confirm = "yes")

result$status
result$report$status
```

`RunAIAnalysis()` is one round: plan, validate, preview, ask, execute, and optionally interpret. Running it again is how you continue — there is no loop option to look for, for the reason given in the previous chapter: the engine executes one plan and never re-plans mid-run.

`result$status` is the execution outcome; `result$report$status` is the planning outcome. They are different fields because they are different questions, and a plan can be fine while an execution fails.

Passing `confirm = "yes"` executes without pausing, which is right for a script and wrong for exploratory use. Leave it out and read the preview first.

## Free-form questions with `sclet_copilot`

Not every question is a plan. `sclet_copilot()` answers a free-form question about an object by reading its recorded provenance — what analysis ran, in what order, with which parameters — instead of looking at the data alone.

```{r ai-in-package-copilot, eval=eval_ai}
sclet_copilot(demo, "I clustered this object after normalization. What should I check before trusting the clusters?")
```

The value here is narrow and worth stating. The tool cannot see your cells; it can see what the ledger recorded and in which order. That is enough to discuss the workflow, and not enough to make a claim about the biology.

## Cross-chain auditing

`AuditAnalysisChain()` asks a narrower question: does the expression of specific genes look distorted by an earlier step? It traces the state machine back to the raw layer and compares.

It needs an integration that produces a corrected **expression** layer. `fastMNN` does, but only when asked for full-gene output — by default it returns a corrected *embedding* and the logical `corrected` layer falls back to the source expression, which is not something to audit:

```{r ai-in-package-audit-setup, eval=eval_chunks}
demo <- RunIntegration(demo, method = "fastMNN", batch = "batch", correct.all = TRUE)

# The logical layer is the vocabulary; the assay behind it is an implementation
# detail that the audit resolves for you.
SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(demo)
```

```{r ai-in-package-audit, eval=eval_ai}
audit <- AuditAnalysisChain(
    demo,
    features = head(rownames(demo), 5),
    raw_layer = "counts",
    integrated_layer = "corrected"
)
cat(audit)
```

**What it returns matters more than what it prints.** The results are recorded with claim levels, and the report's own verification section re-derives them; a round that is not rendered loses that check. Audit output is input to a judgement, not the judgement.

Be aware of which integration method you used:

- `fastMNN` produces a corrected **expression** layer (with `correct.all = TRUE`), so the comparison above is the right abstraction.
- `Harmony` and `scVI` produce a corrected **reduction** — no corrected expression exists to compare against, so this particular audit does not apply and needs adapting.

## What the package will not do

It will not call a provider unless you ask for one explicitly; it will not present a claim stronger than its evidence supports; and it will not treat a successful plan as a successful analysis, because "all steps completed" and "the question was answered" are different statements. The last chapter covers how that difference is enforced.
